data.rationale: Tile the outer row dimension 'i' by 32. This maps 32 rows per block — with M=2048 rows that gives 64 blocks across 30 SMs (≈2.1 waves), maximizing SM utilization while keeping per-block shared memory manageable for the row-wise reduction.

Tile the reduction dimension 'j' by 128. N=2048 elements split into 16 tiles of 128 — each tile fits a warp (128/4 = 32 float4 vectorized loads). This enables 128-bit memory accesses and creates the inner loop structure needed for vectorize and unroll decisions next.

Map the outer 'i' tile to threadblock.x — each CUDA block processes a tile of 32 rows. With 2048/32=64 blocks launched across 30 SMs, this gives full SM utilization and maps naturally to the row-independent parallelism of RMSNorm.

Map the inner 'j' tiles to warps within the block. Each warp handles a 128-element strip of the N=2048 reduction, enabling warp-level shuffle-based reduction (shfl.xor) rather than slower shared-memory atomics. 2048/128=16 warps per block × 32 threads = 512 threads/block — well within the 1024 limit.

Vectorize the j-loop with width=4 (float4 = 128-bit loads). This maximizes memory bandwidth utilization on Ampere (which has 128-bit wide memory buses) and reduces instruction count by 4×. With j-tile=128 and vec=4, each thread issues 128/4=32 vectorized load instructions — a good balance for the instruction cache.

Unroll the j inner loop by 8. With j-tile=128 and vec=4, the innermost loop has 128/4=32 iterations; unrolling by 8 leaves 4 meta-iterations and exposes 8 independent accumulators to the compiler — critical for hiding the 4-cycle FP32 latency on Ampere and saturating the CUDA cores with independent FP ops.

Tile 'i' by 1 — one row per block. With M=2048 rows this launches 2048 blocks, saturating all 30 SMs with ~68 concurrent blocks per SM. This is the canonical RMSNorm/LayerNorm pattern: one block = one row, so all threads within the block cooperate on the single row's reduction, enabling efficient warp shuffles and maximizing parallelism.
